claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a dual-nanoprecipitation microstructure.
APT performed before and after high-temperature oxidation will reveal local elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces.
Elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces largely governs oxidation resistance and degradation mechanisms in Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
Site-specific APT of oxidized cross-sections can provide near-atomic-scale chemical analysis.
Oxidation at 800–1000 °C for 10–100 hours represents conditions relevant to gas-turbine service.
Oxidation-induced diffusion and phase transformations are most pronounced at nanoprecipitate interfaces.
Al may migrate during oxidation to form oxides.
Cr and Ti may redistribute within the matrix during oxidation.
Oxidation can selectively consume an alloying element and deplete that element from the underlying alloy.
APT offers three-dimensional compositional mapping at near-atomic resolution.
APT can elucidate local elemental diffusion pathways during oxidation.
Reactive elements will oxidize preferentially in the target alloy.
Oxidation will change local elemental partitioning around nanoprecipitates.
Local redistribution around nanoprecipitates will lead to new or modified oxide scales.
Oxidation-related redistribution may influence high-temperature mechanical properties.
Longer oxidation times or higher temperatures can alter the relative stability and formation of oxide phases.
Additional thermal-cycling tests may be needed to validate behavior outside the proposed time and temperature range.
Electron microscopy can corroborate oxide-layer thickness and morphology.
Failure to detect any post-oxidation elemental gradient or phase alteration near nanoprecipitates would falsify the proposed redistribution mechanism.
